utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We understand, Ms. Somers, there's been a difficulty with the witness, who is part heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's correct. We were informed by the witness unit this afternoon that Mr. Samardzic is unwell and will not be able to attend today's session. As a result, we mobilised quickly to get the other -- the next witness on the list available. The Defence has been very cooperative. We appreciate the understanding of a situation beyond all our control. And I believe, if the Chamber so approves, the Prosecution, along with Defence's agreement, would be to present the live - I'm sorry - the direct examination, examination-in-chief, of Mr. Grubisic, who would be the next one, and then defer until tomorrow. Perhaps the later start also doesn't necessarily make it a big problem, but we regret that this happened, and there's simply nothing we could accommodate with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Could I indicate that it is possible that we may have to finish a little earlier tomorrow. I mention that now because of what is a growing complexity in your planning of witnesses. We seem to be getting an increasing number of part-heard witnesses. And if it should become relevant, don't feel that you have to have available a witness who can commence in the last hour or hour and a half of tomorrow, if that will help you in your planning. It's a little indefinite yet what the position will be, but the likelihood is that we will need to finish earlier than the normal 7.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I also just ask: If -- well, VWU should probably contact us fairly early, but because the situation can remain somewhat volatile between the first report of okay, if it's the case, and a later time, we will try to stay in the loop amongst this triangle. And if there's any change, we'll make sure that you know as soon as we know, or vice versa, if you learn first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. Now, Mr. Petrovic, it's proposed now to interrupt the evidence of the ill witness and to lead the evidence in chief of Mr. Grubisic. Is that a matter that you're in a position to cope with at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We are aware of the problem, and we appreciate it, and we are prepared, whenever Your Honour so orders, to begin our cross-examination of Witness Samardzic, of course, after Ms. Somers completes her examination-in-chief. With regard to the witness Grubisic, bearing in mind the expeditiousness of the trial, we are prepared for this witness to be examined in direct examination today and to cross-examine this witness tomorrow. It would be very useful for us to know whether this is the plan or whether there is any possibility of Mr. Samardzic coming back tomorrow. Am I asking something that is hard to establish at the present time? If it isn't, then -- or if it is, I would like to know when we will find out whether Mr. Samardzic is able to testify tomorrow or not, and for how long, in view of his health and the number of questions that the cross-examination will have to cover of Mr. Samardzic. And also, bearing in mind what Your Honour has said, that tomorrow the session might end earlier. We would like to establish some sort of mechanism as to when we will learn what is to follow. This is our only request. And we will be as cooperative as possible in this whole matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your indications, Mr. Petrovic. As I understand the position from Ms. Somers, the availability of Mr. Samardzic will depend upon his health. It is not yet known whether he will be well enough to attend tomorrow. It is our expectation that as soon as he is well enough, he will be here for his cross-examination. So if you can remain in a state of preparation for his cross-examination. With the witness Mr. Grubisic, I understand from you now that you are not today ready to cross-examine him, but if you could be prepared by tomorrow to cross-examine him. It is not yet clear, and it can't be clear today, whether it will be Mr. Samardzic or Mr. Grubisic, or perhaps even both, who will be available tomorrow. But if we could ask you to be ready to deal with one or other of them, or both of them, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as our preparedness is concerned, we will be prepared, but I'm not sure we will have sufficient time to do both in the course of tomorrow. However, we will be prepared to do this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, we fully appreciate that to deal with both may be expecting too much, especially as the Chamber may well need to finish early, as I have indicated. But your need to be prepared should be to be prepared to cross-examine either or both Mr. Samardzic or Mr. Grubisic, because we can't be sure today whether or not Mr. Samardzic will be well enough tomorrow to attend Court. Well, thank you for that. Now, if you could proceed with the next witness, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If Mr. Grubisic could take the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Grubisic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, could you state your name, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Slavko Grubisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you live.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: In Dubrovnik, Celestin Medovica Street number 4, and for four years now I have occasionally been going to the island of Sipan over the weekend, Saturday, Sunday, and Mondays.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us how old you are and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: 65, the 22nd of May, 1938.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us: How are you employed, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I am a priest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of what religion, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us how you're currently serving as a Roman Catholic priest.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: On the island of Sipan as I have already said, I spend three days there, and the rest of the time I'm in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long have you been a priest, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Forty years. Last summer I celebrated my 40th anniversary, because I was ordained in 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your first assignment was in 1963?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: My first assignment was as a catechist in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what is a catechist?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: A teacher of religion, of religious education. I taught religious education. At that time it was not taught in schools but only in the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you also serve as a rector at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I was not a parish priest, but I was appointed rector of four churches in the Old Town in Dubrovnik, St. Joseph, St. Rocco, St. Domino, and the church of St. Nicholas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's talk about those churches, just briefly. Let's start off with St. Joseph's. Could you tell us where that's located in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: In the Od Puca Street, but there is no number, because churches do not have house numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Right. Could you tell us when the church was built, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: On the spot where the church of St. Joseph stands today, there was appear church previously. I think it was St. James. But in 1667, it was destroyed in an earthquake, and after that, the present-day church of St. Joseph was built. Therefore, it dates back to the seventeenth century.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how the church of St. Joseph has been used since 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: It was used when there was a larger number of priests, to celebrate mass once a week. Now it is used only occasionally, because there are fewer priests available, so that usually funeral services are held there. Sometimes once a week or several times a week, and sometimes weeks will go by without any mass being celebrated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on to St. Rocco church. Could you tell us what street that's on in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: It's in the street that is named after St. Rocco. It's called Za Rokom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us when that church was built?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: It was also built -- well, it was built in the sixteenth century, a little earlier than the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how was that used at this time, or how has it been used since 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: In 1979, there was an earthquake in Dubrovnik, and this church was damaged in the earthquake. After this, because the cathedral had also been damaged, many objects from the cathedral were removed to this church. So that since 1979, it has not been used as a church, to celebrate mass or religious services, but as a storage area for the remains of the old altar from the cathedral and other church furniture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us move to Church Domino. Could you tell us where that's located in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: It is in the Od Domina Street at the top of Siroka Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where was that first built?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: This church was mentioned as early as the twelfth century, but later on it was demolished and rebuilt, but it actually dates back to the twelfth century.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And since 1991, how has that church been used?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: It is used only at Christmas, because Christmas masses are celebrated there, at Christmastime, over a 15-day period. Local tambure musicians play there and sing traditional Christmas carols and I can tell you that at Christmastime this is the most frequently visited church in Dubrovnik, although it's not large. During the rest of the year it's used to hold religious education classes or various meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now let's move to the final of the four churches that you served as a rector beginning in 1963. The church of St. Nikola, could you tell us where that's located in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: The church of St. Nicholas is in Prijeko Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when that was constructed or built?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: This is one of the oldest churches. The first church was mentioned in the eleventh century, and after the earthquake in 1979, it was restored and excavated, and a church was found, which is now underneath the floor, which dates back to the eleventh century. This church was rebuilt several times, I think three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how was that church used, and how has it been used since 1991, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: The church is used for mass or liturgy only on the holiday of St. Nicholas on the 6th of December. During the rest of the year it's used for choir practice by the cathedral choir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, in October of 1991, were you living at Celestina Medovica Street number 4?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who else was living in that building?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Besides myself, on the floor below, because this building has two floors, a basement and an attic, the first two floors were used by the late Don Ante Dracevac and I lived on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say Ante Dracevac, is that Father Dracevac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who was living with you on the second floor, I believe?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: He was a priest like me. I didn't understand your question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That was my question, whether or not he was a priest. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, who else was living with you in the apartment in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of October, or rather, the day before, I received a phone call from a friend and colleague of mine, the late Don Milan Majic, who was a parish priest in Brgat and Postranje. He told me that his village was being shelled, and asked if he could come and stay with me. My niece, Marija Lemo who lived in Mlini also asked if she could come and stay with me, because she couldn't sleep because of the shelling. I told them to come. Don Milan arrived, so did my niece, her husband Ante, and their three daughters. She also brought two other families with them, a Serbian family, Dusko Tomovic, his wife Slavka and their two sons, and also the Mioc family. The wife's name was Angela. She was a Serb. And her husband was called Vinko. And their two children. There were 15 of us all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why weren't these people living in their own homes, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Because shelling had started, and they came to stay with me, hoping to go back to their homes. But unfortunately, they were no longer able to return home, and so they stayed with me, all of them, for over a month. And only later, when the siege of Dubrovnik was lifted, did the women and children leave the town and leave in the direction of Split. The men stayed in the house, together with Slavka Tomovic, the Serb lady, and her husband Dusko, while their sons, in the meantime, had joined the HVO. The women and children left for Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what the HVO is, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: The Croatian army, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to yourself, were there other residents in the Old Town who took in refugees that were friends or relatives?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some people like that, but not so many in the Old Town, because the houses were not large enough. People received their families and friends, but most of the refugees from Mlini, Mandaljina, Brgat, and Postranje, came to the hotels.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about October and the happenings to the Old Town. Could you talk about what happened to the power in October?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of October, in the morning, we heard shelling and gunfire. On that day, there was a power failure because the transformer station in Komolac had been hit. There was also no water, because the water depends on the electricity. The relay on Srdj was also hit, so that we no longer had communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a siege. Was Dubrovnik under siege during the month of October?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both from the land and the sea and the air. We were besieged on all sides. Our bishop, in the letters he sent out in those days, referred to Dubrovnik as the largest concentration camp in the world because it had about 60.000 inhabitants at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say Dubrovnik, you're referring to the full municipality, not just the Old Town, the 60.000 inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: The Old Town, Lapad, Gruz, and Dubrovnik proper. The entire municipality has about -- well, I'm talking to the -- about the diocese, actually. The diocese has about 70.000 people, believers. But I think Dubrovnik has 35.000, but very many refugees had gathered in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell the Court: Was the Old Town of Dubrovnik shelled in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure. Was the Old Town of Dubrovnik shelled in 1991, October?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was. This happened on the 5th of October. Don Milan Majic and I went to the Lero hotel, where refugees were accommodated, mostly from his parish. On our way back, the shelling began, and we took shelter, as far as we were able to. There was an air raid warning being sounded. And when we came to the entrance to the town, for the first time I saw that the Spile [as interpreted] Gate leading to the town was closed. In the 40 years I had lived in Dubrovnik, that gate had never been closed. We went in through a small opening in the gate, and we noticed that shrapnel was falling. When we took shelter in the cellar, after the shelling, we saw that the Rupe museum had been hit and a building in Rudjer Boskova Street. No. I apologise. Yes, yes, it was Rudjer Boskova Street, because there is also a Rudjer Boskovic square, so that was the reason for my confusion. But it was in Rudjer Boskovic Street in Prijeko. We refer to it locally as the Od Bruze [phoen] Street because there's an exit from the town leading from there. There are only three exits from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's take them one building at a time. First the Rupe museum. Where was it hit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: The roof was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the building on Rudjer Boskovica Street, where was that hit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: That building was hit sideways, just above the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the transcript, it says "the Spile gate". Is that "Pile," Pile gate?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes, Pile.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you had been outside when the shelling began, sir. Did you see any Croatian troops in the Old Town while the shelling was occurring in October?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand the first question. Was I where?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were outdoors when the shelling began, coming back from the hotel Lero?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you observe any Croatian troops in the Old Town when the shelling was occurring?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Not only did I observe no troops, I never saw any troops inside the Old Town, or outside the walls, for that matter. There were no Croatian soldiers around at the time. It was only later that some soldiers came over. But at that time there were no soldiers around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see any artillery pieces or mortars in the Old Town in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Not only did I not see any at that time, but never. I've been in Dubrovnik for 40 years, and I had been to school for five years before that. I never saw any weapons inside the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, did you see anyone firing any type of weapon or object from the Old Town, firing out from the Old Town in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us move to November of 1991. Was there any shelling of the Old Town in the month of November?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were four days of general alert. I believe it was on the 10th, 11th, 12th, and 13th of November. Not many shells fell on the Old Town, though, in those four days, although the general alert was on and life was difficult because we had to spend those four days in our cellars, and we lacked the basic means of subsistence in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during that time period, I'm again going to ask you if you saw any troops or artillery or mortars in the Old Town in November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any police officers in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how were they armed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: They were armed, as policemen usually are. They were carrying pistols. It was only once, though, that I saw, at Porporela, two police officers who were sort of standing guard there, and they had automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the first officers that you saw. How often did you see officers, police officers, in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Well, the usual thing, the sort of thing that police do in any other town. They just go about their regular duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were there many police officers in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on that one occasion you saw two police officers with rifles, were those local officers? Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Those were the same ones who were there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were they firing those rifles?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said you saw them at Porporela. Is that the pensioners' building out in the harbour?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: You have the town harbour, and there are two piers. The big pier is used for ships to dock, and probably those two were standing guard there to prevent any ships from docking, one of the ships that were blocking us. There was not much they could do there. They were just there for some sort of basic security, nothing else, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us move to December of 1991. You're still living at the Old Town, in that same home?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on or about -- or actually, let me step back. How did you receive your daily information in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: As I've said, there was no electricity, no power, but we did have radio sets, and we listened to Radio Dubrovnik, to news on Radio Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you hear any announcements on or about the 5th of December, 1991? Tell the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes. The news said that our negotiators had left for Cavtat to negotiate with the JNA. It was said that an agreement had been reached about a ceasefire, and we were very glad and pleasantly surprised to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they say whether or not it had been signed, this agreement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: They said it had not been signed yet but that it would be signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they say why the agreement hadn't been signed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Truth to tell, I can't quite remember now why. I don't think I can answer this question with any degree of precision whatsoever. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, let's move to the next day, December 6th. Does that have any significance to you for any religious purpose?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Of course it does. That's St. Nikola's Day. As I said before when we spoke about the church of St. Nicholas, we have mass in that church on that day. This is the only day in the entire year when mass is celebrated in that church. I happened to be the rector of that church. There was supposed to be mass celebrated at 7, 8, 9, 10.00, 11.00, 12.00, and at 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that a festive day? Do a lot of people attend mass on that date?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: It's not a mandatory holiday, not a holiday of obligation. This has to do with sailors, St. Nicholas being the patron saint of sailors. St. Nicholas Day is especially important for children. It is their day, when children receive presents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said that masses were scheduled for -- several masses for scheduled for that date. Was there any announcement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where was it announced that masses would be scheduled on that date?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: This was announced. We usually announce this while celebrating mass, with a week's notice. But as this is a holiday for all, I made -- I asked the radio station to announce this with a week's notice, that mass would be celebrated. So Radio Dubrovnik announced what would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move to December 6th. Can you tell us where you were in the early morning hours, about 5.00, 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I was in bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did something happen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: About half past 5.00 - I can't be certain about the exact time. I think it was about half past 5.00 - heavy firing began. My friend and I, and all the other people who were in my house, we got up, and as you can see the Imperial hotel and the Pile gate from my window, the one we referred to, we saw shells falling on the hotel and on the Dubrovnik cafe. We sprang to our feet immediately, threw some clothes on, and ran down to the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said the Imperial hotel was shelled.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is the Imperial hotel located within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How far is the Imperial hotel from the walls of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Well, less than a hundred metres, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what about the Dubrovka [sic] Cafe by the gate?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: The Dubrovnik cafe. Ten metres, perhaps. Ten to fifteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you ran down to the cellar. How long did you stay in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: We stayed while the shelling continued. It stopped at about 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you go outside prior to 3.00, while the shelling was occurring?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: You couldn't even keep your eyes open, let alone leave the cellar. Let me just illustrate this. There was a shell that hit the monastery of the friars, or Little Brethren, and there is an old chemists' which was about ten metres from ours. We had a candle that provided light for us in the cellars. The explosion was so strong that it blew the flame out. Therefore, it was entirely impossible for us to even ponder the possibility of leaving the cellar and coming out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you hear the explosions as you remained in the cellar between 6.00 and 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Even a deaf man would have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, about 3.00 p.m., the shelling stops. What do you do?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Well, the first thing we did was come out to see what was going on, to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: We observed that there was smoke in the whole town. The town was shrouded in smoke. The nearby building where the headquarters of the Dubrovnik festival were - this is at the bottom of my street, just that you approach it from a different street, from the Zigurate street - we saw that this building was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that building known as the Festival Palace?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I believe so. The Festival Palace, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: The men started out. We had a ladder. We shattered the window and entered the building. The attic was on fire inside the building, we realised. Two men got into the building through the window, and they were passing things from the building through the window, for us to take them away, mostly technical appliances or paintings, pieces of furniture. We were able to salvage a number of different things from inside the house. They were grateful to us later for having done what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do with this property that you removed from the Festival Palace?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: We put them away in my cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you able to remove all the property from that building and save it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: No, not all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Just some. We couldn't, for the simple reason that shelling resumed soon after. There was a lull, which lasted between 3.00 and 5.00, and then shelling resumed and we ran back to the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you returned to the cellar, and do you remain there for a while?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes. We remained until as late as 8.00, when the shelling stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did do you after that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, I forgot to say, my house had been hit also. The roof was hit by a shell. The diameter of the hole was about four metres, the hole in the roof. The roof had caved in. After that, at about 8.00 p.m., we came out, reached the bottom of the street, where, as I said a while ago, the Festival building is. It was still on fire. On the ground floor of that building, there is a cafe, a coffee house, called Manon. Some other people from the building had arrived in the meantime and started to take things out from the cafe, and they started leaving these things outside on the main street, on Stradun to keep these things from burning down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you help these people with removing the property?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I helped. Mr. Djelo Jusic, who is a local composer, was also around, and he helped too. There were quite a number of us there giving a hand. I think some even recorded the scene with their cameras.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that a shell had fallen through your roof and left a four-metre-diameter hole.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How do you know it was a shell that went through the roof, or a projectile of some type?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I know because we found -- I'm not sure what you call that. I think you call it the tail of the shell. It was a low-calibre shell. That's what I was told. I preserved it. It was an 82-millimetre shell. Because you have that bigger kind of shell too, with greater destructive power, which I believe is 120 millimetres. This was a lower-calibre shell. Otherwise it would have gone straight down to the cellar. And this way, it only damaged the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to make it clear for the record: Your house and the Festival Palace, those are both within the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were outside on those two occasions on December 6th, did you see any Croatian soldiers or artillery or mortars firing out of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Never. As I said before, not only did I not see anyone on that day, but not ever, not once.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone firing from the walls or firing out of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let us move on to December 7th. Did you walk through the Old Town on December 7th?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What time did you begin your tour of the Old Town on the 7th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: At about 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I went through almost the entire town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you observe as you started to walk?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I must say that this was one of the most difficult moments in my life. I cried like a child once I had surveyed everything. First when I reached Stradun, I saw debris lying around, roof tiles, shattered glass, rubble. There was hardly space for you to walk amid the rubble. The whole street was littered, the main street, Stradun. The situation was more or less the same throughout the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you visit the churches that you served as rector in, those four churches?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I visited the four churches and everything else: The cathedral, St. Blaze's church, and all the other churches, all of them. Not only the churches. I saw a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's start on your tour of Dubrovnik on that morning. Which church did you visit first?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: When I first left Stradun I took Siroka Ulica, Siroka Street. The first thing I saw was terrifying. There was a palace where Ivo Grbic, a painter, lives, and this palace had been gutted and totally burned down. Then you have the All Saints church, a bit further on down the street. I looked at the church, and it was a terrifying sight, a dreadful sight. A shell had fallen just outside the church, destroying the steps in front of the church. Two of the side windows had been broken through and shattered completely. The rose window above the portal, the round window above the portal, the diameter must be between 150 and 180 centimetres, so the rose window had been totally demolished. The door to the church was still in place, but, as I said, a shell had destroyed the steps, and the door was pimpled with shrapnel. Once I went inside the church, I saw that a shell had hit the roof. I couldn't see a hole in the roof, but I saw the results down on the floor. The shell had penetrated through the roof and hit the floor and damaged the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were there any windows on that building, other than the round window over the door?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: As I said before, there were two windows, and both window had been shattered completely, thrown off the hinges and completely useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that it was the All Saints church. Is that also the Domino church? Is that also called the Domino church?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: The name of the church is actually Domino, which is short for Deo et omnibus sanctis, All Saints. So Domino is just short for Deo et omnibus sanctis, God and All Saints. We all refer to it as the Domino church.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what about the walls to the building? Was there any shrapnel damage or shell damage to the walls of the Domino church?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes. The portal of the church, because the steps had been demolished, and you can still see traces. I was never asked the question, but later, later on - it was in late May or early June - the church was hit from the side. So that four or five metres inside the church, there was shattered stone which fell from the window. But this was not the case with St. Nikola's church this time around. This happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us stick with December 1991 right now. After you finished looking at the Domino church, or the All Saints church, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I went to Puce Street and went towards St. Joseph church.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you observe then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: The first thing I saw when looking at St. Joseph's church, on the front of the church you have St. Joseph's statue. It wasn't completely destroyed, but it had been decapitated. The right arm was missing, and some of the cloak had been damaged by shrapnel, although the church did not at that time receive a direct hit, but rather a shell fell just across the way, hit a terrace across the way, damaging the statue and the windows which had been shot, obviously, and, as a consequence, shattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you able to find the head, the arm, and part of the cloak of St. Joseph, of the statue of St. Joseph?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I was not able to find them. I found only fragments, which I put in a box. We put those fragments away. And later, the statue of St. Joseph was restored. An artist put those fragments together as best he could, but where there were bits missing, because we hadn't found the pieces, he filled that in with gypsum and he fashioned a new head, which we put into the church, with an inscription saying that it had been damaged during the attack on Dubrovnik on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when the statue was repaired?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but an American gave me $5,000 to have the statue repaired. And a sculptor named Ivankovic repaired it. I think this was five or six years after the event. I have this information among my documents, but I couldn't tell you off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were any other buildings damaged in the vicinity of St. Joseph's Church?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: After this happened in the church, I once said that St. Joseph had sacrificed his head but preserved the church, because the palaces on either side of the church were burnt to the ground. They had been hit with incendiary projectiles and they burnt to the ground, both of them. And a third palace opposite the Orthodox church, they were all next to each other, they were all adjacent, and they all burnt down to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Speaking of the Orthodox church, do you know if that suffered any damage?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only on the roof: I was not able to see that on that day. From outside you couldn't see any damage. But when I returned home later, I could see that it had been -- that it had been hit by two shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: After this, I continued down Od Puca Street, over Gundulic Plain, and came to the rector's palace, and then continued on towards the cathedral.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you observe as you walked?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, there was rubble everywhere, debris. The whole town was littered with this. At the rector's palace, as far as I was able to see from the outside, because a shell had landed between the cathedral and the rector's palace, from the north, or rather, the south side, from the cathedral, on those beautiful stones, there are still marks made by shrapnel. It's pock-marked by shrapnel still. Another shell landed next to the cathedral and hit a palace, where a priest had resided. His name was Don Marko Herendija. And there were other people who lived in that building. That shell had hit the corner of the building, right next to the window. And there were a lot of holes, a lot of pockmarks on the cathedral from the shrapnel from that shell, which are still there, because it's only three metres away. On the dome of the cathedral, between the windows, a shell had hit the ornaments on the facade, and the stones had fallen down. But fortunately, the cathedral was covered in lead and there are wooden boards underneath. These pieces of stone had hit the lead and fallen down onto the terrace, where we collected them later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After you completed your observations of the cathedral, where else did you go?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Let me just add: I went into the cathedral to see what had happened inside. There was no damage inside the cathedral, but pieces of shrapnel had entered above the door. Then I went to St. Blaze's church and saw something dreadful. The balustrade in front of the church, a beautiful balustrade, on the side facing the rector's palace was totally demolished. At the sides of the entrance gate, to the left and the right, there were two coats of arms. About a metre and a half by one metre in size. One shell had shattered the left-hand side coat of arms. It has now been restored, I think by the French, who provided the funds and restored it, to match the coat of arms on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said St. Blaze's church. Does that go under other names too?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Not in our area. This is Sanctus Blazius, and on the coats of arms of the Dubrovnik Republic, it always says Sanctus Blazius, St. Blaze. In Dubrovnik, he's locally referred to as Vlaho. In Zagreb, if you mentioned St. Vlaho, people would find it funny. If in Dubrovnik, if were you to say St. Blaze, people would laugh. Locally he's referred to as St. Vlaho but this is St. Blazius who lived in Armenia and became the patron saint of Dubrovnik in the tenth century and since then has been venerated as the patron saint of Dubrovnik. And his feast day is celebrated with great solemnity. It was a very sumptuous celebration on the 3rd of February every year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the other two churches you serve as rector, St. Nicholas and St. Rocco, could you tell us what, if any, damage those churches suffered?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: A bit of damage. They were not hit directly, but they suffered damage from shrapnel, or bits of stone falling from other buildings. On St. Nikola's Day, the worst damage was done to the part called Prijeko. That's where the most shells fell. They landed all over the town. I don't know exactly, but people say that over a thousand shells landed on the town that day. And the part that was least affected was called Karmen, where St. John's fortress is and the aquarium. That's where the least shells landed. However, these two churches were not hit directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you familiar with a small church on Od Zigurate Street?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Of course I am. It's right next to where I live. It's one of the older churches of Dubrovnik. It's well known that Dubrovnik is a UNESCO protected site. The whole town is a cultural monument. But this church was especially well known. And on St. Nikola's Day, it was hit by one of the larger-calibre shells, because we found its tail, as I just described a while ago, so that we could see it was a larger calibre. Thanks to many good people, the church has by now been restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe the damage as best you can, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: It's a small church. When a large-calibre projectile hit its roof, it had a little dome, and this was just blown apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, not far from there is the Franciscan monastery.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what, if any, damage, the Franciscan monastery suffered.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether on that day alone, but over 50 shells hit this monastery all together. That day, it suffered a lot of damage. The church was hit several times. I could see that from my window, from the window of my flat. The cloister of the brethren, where the oldest pharmacy in Europe is located, was also damaged, the bell tower was damaged. I forgot to tell you that the bell tower, the town bell tower, at the entrance towards Porporela, is looks like a church bell tower, but it isn't. Anyone who has visited Dubrovnik would know what it looks like. That too was hit in the cupola, in the dome. In front of the Church of the Friar's Minor, there was a well. We call it Onofrio's fountain. It's something very special in Dubrovnik. It is covered by a dome. And this dome was hit in two places. The dome was made of old tiles, and later, when it was restored, I was fortunate enough to be able to help, because in my attic, the floor was made of old bricks which were used to protect the house from fire. And I took out several square metres of these old bricks and replaced them with concrete, and then I donated them for the restoration of the fountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to cover two other subjects, then show you a map. Do you know a man -- or did you know a man by the name of Pavo Urban, a young man?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Pavo Urban. Yes, I did know him. He was a photographer, a young man. He was killed on that day. Just below the town bell tower. But I have to say, I didn't see his body. I know that he was killed on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was he killed within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes, within the Old Town, just under the bell tower and the Sponza Palace.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say he was killed on that day, are you referring to December 6th, when the Old Town was shelled?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The 6th of December. I apologise. Yes. Because we were already talking about the 7th. He was killed on the 6th, yes. On the 7th I was able to go out, because there was already a lull.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did he belong to your church or to another church?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: He was a parishioner of St. Peter's at Boninovo, where our cemetery is, Don Pero Vuletic is the parish priest of his parish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you perform the burial service or the burial mass for Mr. Urban, or did someone from the other church perform it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't I who did that. I don't know who did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to ask you about an officer in the Yugoslavian navy, a Captain Jeremic. Did you ever meet with this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met him in the city harbour. I don't know what date it was exactly. But it was certainly before the attack on the Old Town. About a month after the first shelling we experienced. But I don't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you tell us about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I heard that he was coming to the city harbour. He arrived in Ivica Herendija's boat and I went with a lady called Vesna. I don't know her last name. She is a tourist guide. She is a Serb. And Mario Bonic, who was then a coach of the Dubrovnik football club, soccer club. And we came to see him. I said to him: "I'm a Catholic priest. Are you Sofronije Jeremic?" He said: "Yes, I am." I said: "For a month now -- well, up to a month ago, we lived in peace and harmony and love. Since your arrival, since you encircled our town, we have been living under impossible conditions, without water, without power, without staple foodstuffs or basic necessities." I said: "What kind of opinion can we have of you when we hear on our transistor radios that Sofronije Jeremic ordered the food that was to arrive by these ships to be thrown away?" And he replied: "I'm only carrying out orders. I have to do this." I don't remember the entire conversation, but Mato Jerinic, a journalist from Dubrovnik, wrote about it in the newspaper, and I think that there is a record of this. And then that Serb lady told him -- the Serb lady said to him: "I am a Serb. If you ask me whether I am in any danger, I will say yes, but I was not in danger before you encircled us. I have been in danger since you encircled us."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, what position did Captain Jeremic tell you he held?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask him that, but I read that he was, I think, a liaison captain or -- he was a liaison officer between the Crisis Staff and the negotiators of the international community. I think his title was liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said you cannot recall the date in which you spoke with Captain Jeremic, the liaison officer for the JNA. If I showed you your statement and you were able to look at that, do you think you would be able to refresh your recollection as to the date?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the usher please show the statement of Father Grubisic. And I invite your attention to page 3 in the B/C/S version, paragraph 13, or it's the highlighted paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just read it to yourself, please, sir. Would you look at the highlighted portion first, the yellow section.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I was looking at the wrong part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Having read that, does that refresh your recollection as to the date that you had this meeting or conversation with the liaison officer, Captain Jeremic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of October, 1991. But I wish to add something in connection with this. I promised at the beginning to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The only reserve I have is that I may be unable to remember precise dates. However, everything else is what I have experienced and seen with my own eyes, and that is absolutely the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown a copy of Exhibit 13, which we'd like to have this witness mark and then tender as 13 -- either A or however the registrar would like it numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I mention, Mr. Weiner, that when the time comes, it seems preferable to give it a completely new exhibit number rather than a branch of Exhibit 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the area depicted in that map?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: The Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please find your home on that map, the location of your home.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Celestina Medovica, the first entrance next to the Prijeko Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you put a "1" next to the area where your home is, right on the area.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please find the area where the St. Joseph's Church is located.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you put a "2" next to that dot, where you indicated the St. Joseph's Church is located.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you find the area where St. Rocco's Church is located.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you please place a "3" next to St. Rocco's Church.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you find the area where the Domino or All Saints Church is located.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you place a "4" next to that

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you find the area where the St. Nicholas Church is located.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you place a "5" next to the St. Nicholas Church.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you find the Rupe museum.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you place a "6" next to that, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please find the Orthodox Church.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you place a "7" next to the Orthodox Church.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please find the cathedral.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you place an "8" next to the cathedral.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you find the small church at Od Zigurate Street that was damaged.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you place a "9" next to that dot.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you find the monastery, the Franciscan monastery, which you saw from your house had been damaged.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you place a "10" next to that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you find the bell clock tower, either the clock tower or the bell tower, that had a shell hit its cupola.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you place an "11" next to that, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you find the building on Rudjer Boskovic Street. You said the walls were damaged at the shelling in October.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you place a "12" next to that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you show us St. Blaze's, or if you want to call it, Vlaho or Basil's [sic] Church, the church of the patron saint of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you place a "13" next to that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, could you find or show the area where the domed fountain is, just outside of the Franciscan monastery.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you place a "14" next to that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GRUBISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That completes the examination-in-chief of this witness. I would like to offer this map, with the various locations identified, as the Prosecution's next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P30.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one housekeeping matter before --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just one housekeeping matter. Mr. Grubisic has to say mass this weekend on that island, and if -- regardless of the situation with Mr. Samardzic -- or let's assume Mr. Samardzic is here tomorrow and is well and is testifying, could this witness please complete his testimony first so we can get him off and back to Dubrovnik so he can say mass this weekend?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems to be no difficulty with that, Mr. Weiner, so Don Grubisic ought to be able to get away tomorrow. We will, then, in accordance with the discussion earlier today, adjourn now for the day and resume tomorrow at 2.15, we hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of January 2004, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.13 p.m.,
